title: 3.4.15 Plain English to Pseudocode: Decision Tree for Form Choice
description: Turn the rule for choosing a function form into pseudocode: is it a main operation called from several places, and if not, is its body a single expression?

planChart.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A([choosing a function form starts]) --> B[/read in the job of the function/]
  B --> C{called from several places?}
  C -- yes --> D[write a function declaration]
  C -- no --> E{is the body a single expression?}
  E -- yes --> F[write a one-line arrow with implicit return]
  E -- no --> G[write an arrow with a block body and return]
  D --> Z([the form is chosen])
  F --> Z
  G --> Z
planChart.caption: the form rule: the first diamond decides the declaration, the second splits the two arrow forms, and every path ends at the same chosen form.

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** Read in the job of the function.

**2.** If it is a main operation called from several places, write a function **declaration**.

**3.** Otherwise, ask whether its body is a single expression. If it is, write a **one-line arrow** with an implicit return.

**4.** If it is not, write an **arrow with a block body** and an explicit `return`.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: the first diamond is the "called from several places" question, the second is the "single expression" question, and every path ends at the same chosen form.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `SET lives TO 3` (start a value)
- `IF lives is 0` ... `END IF` (a check, with the steps inside it indented)
- `RETURN lives` (the answer)
- `FOR EACH coin IN coins` ... `END FOR` (repeat for every item)

Plain English is fine here. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, test three cases by hand: a named `main()` called from five places; a one-expression callback; a helper that needs several statements. Each must reach exactly one form.
hints: Two questions, one after the other: where is it called from, then what does the body look like.
Each of the three forms needs its own step, so there are three different results.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: Asks if it is called from several places
requirements.description: Ask whether the function is a main operation called from several places.
requirements.hint: Add a question about where the function is called from: is it a main operation called from several places?

requirements.title: Asks if the body is a single expression
requirements.description: Ask whether the function body is a single expression.
requirements.hint: Add a second question about the body: is it a single expression?

requirements.title: A declaration for the main operation
requirements.description: Write a function declaration for the main operation.
requirements.hint: Say that the main operation gets a function declaration.

requirements.title: A one-line arrow for a single expression
requirements.description: Write a one-line arrow with an implicit return when the body is a single expression.
requirements.hint: Say that a single-expression body becomes a one-line arrow with an implicit return.

requirements.title: A block-body arrow for the rest
requirements.description: Write an arrow with a block body and an explicit return for everything else.
requirements.hint: Say that anything longer becomes an arrow with a block body and a return.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given a four-step plain-English rule for choosing how to write a function and rewrote it as numbered pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The rule: read in the job of the function; if it is a main operation called from several places, write a function declaration; otherwise, if its body is a single expression, write a one-line arrow with an implicit return; otherwise write an arrow with a block body and an explicit return. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, WRITE, PRINT, RETURN, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite. Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Numbered steps
rubric.description: The student numbered their steps (1. 2. 3. or similar), at least four of them.

rubric.title: Asks if it is called from several places
rubric.description: The steps ask whether the function is a main operation called from several places (or an equivalent wording).

rubric.title: Asks if the body is a single expression
rubric.description: The steps ask whether the function body is a single expression (or just one line / one thing).

rubric.title: A declaration for the main operation
rubric.description: The steps say that the main operation called from several places is written as a function declaration.

rubric.title: A one-line arrow for a single expression
rubric.description: The steps say that a single-expression body is written as a one-line arrow with an implicit return (no braces, no return word).

rubric.title: A block-body arrow for the rest
rubric.description: The steps say that a longer body is written as an arrow with a block body and an explicit return.
